5.2a — The Door: Breaking In with Events

You have an axe; the cave door does not care — yet. Today you wire the last gap shut: press E near a lever, the lever fires a UnityEvent, and the door opens without the lever ever knowing what a door is. That gap between cause and effect is called abstraction, and it is the most AP-exam-flavored idea in the whole starter.

Predict First ~10 min

Read the player half of the interaction — PlayerController.Update:

if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E))
{
    Lever[] levers = FindObjectsByType<Lever>(FindObjectsSortMode.None);
    foreach (Lever lever in levers)
    {
        if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, lever.transform.position) < 2.0f)
        {
            lever.Interact();
        }
    }
}

And the lever's whole personality — Lever.cs:

[SerializeField] private UnityEvent onLeverOn;
[SerializeField] private UnityEvent onLeverOff;

public void Interact()
{
    isOn = !isOn; // Toggle state
    if (isOn)
    {
        if (spriteRenderer != null && onSprite != null) spriteRenderer.sprite = onSprite;
        onLeverOn.Invoke();
    }
    else
    {
        if (spriteRenderer != null && offSprite != null) spriteRenderer.sprite = offSprite;
        onLeverOff.Invoke();
    }
}

Predict: the word "door" appears nowhere in Lever.cs. How can a lever open a door it has never met? Which window would you open to teach the lever about the door — and what does that say about where the "game rules" actually live?

Socratic

The AP exam calls a procedure that calls other procedures without knowing their names abstraction — the same word as the Create PT's "manage complexity." What complexity does UnityEvent manage here — write down what the lever WOULD have needed to know otherwise.

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — the 2-unit social contract. Press E anywhere: the code finds EVERY lever and asks each one "within 2.0 units of me?" — the same Distance pattern as the turret (3.1a), pointed inward instead of outward. Stand near the cave door's lever and press E: sprite swaps (onSprite), isOn flips, and the UnityEvent fires. Press E again: everything un-fires. Toggles are honest machines — every cause has a reverse.

Step 2 — wire the door, no code. Select the Switch/lever object near the cave entrance. In the Inspector find On Lever On (the UnityEvent). The plus button adds a listener: drag the DOOR GameObject into the slot, choose what to call on it — GameObject → SetActive(false) for a vanishing door, or destroy it, or play an animation. Run: press E near it. The door obeys. You just changed the game's rules from the Inspector, with zero lines of code.

Step 3 — respect the gate. Here is the design contract the next lesson honors: the door should only open for the axe-holder. Does the lever check hasAxe? No — the lever checks nothing. Where SHOULD the check live: the lever, the door, or the player? Write your answer; tomorrow's cave lesson (5.3a) takes the door off its hinges anyway, so argue it as a designer would.

Bug Hunt: The event that wouldn't

  1. Walk away 5 units and press E. What does the foreach-_distance combo protect you from — and what would pressing E do EVERYWHERE without it?
  2. Wire the door's SetActive(false) into On Lever Off instead of On. Now what is the E-press sequence to get in — and is that a puzzle or a bug?
  3. Leave the lever's onSprite field empty. Does the event still fire? What does that tell you about the sprite swap and the event — which is decoration and which is the machinery?
  4. Add a SECOND lever and stand between them (both within 2 units). Press E once — what happened, and should one keypress ever flip two switches?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Event design

  1. Wire the lever to TWO listeners: open the door AND play a sound/animation. Does the lever notice? Why is "whoever wants to know, listens" the scalable direction?
  2. Make a FALSE wall: the lever opens a secret passage instead of the cave. How many lines of code did that cost?
  3. Hard: make the lever only work when hasAxe is true. Which script gains an if — and can you do it with zero changes to Lever.cs?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain UnityEvents as cause-and-effect with a gap: the lever never names the door
  • Wire a listener in the Inspector and change game rules with no code
  • Explain the E-key interaction: FindObjectsByType + Distance < 2.0
  • Argue where an item-gate check belongs
